Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action:
Three Negative Results for Pre-Action Misalignment Monitoring

 

Max Fomin  Elad David  Amit LeVi 

Zenity

††footnotetext: Correspondence to: Max Fomin <maxf@zenity.io>.
Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026. Copyright 2026 by the author(s).
Abstract

Probes on model internals could help monitor agentic systems if they identify harmful text or tool actions before those actions are generated. We ask when an internal readout supports this stronger pre-action claim, rather than merely describing the prompt, construction contrast, or current trajectory. We test three methods across three model families: a Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct fine-tune/base direction, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes at the last token of unsafe prefills, and Gemma-3-27B-IT emotion-concept vectors used for projection and steering in a blackmail tool-action scenario. Across these cases, construction validity, semantic legibility, and steering effects do not become robust pre-action monitors: each is undercut by a generalization or specificity check. The Qwen direction separates fine-tune from base at AUC 1.0001.000, yet crosses its threshold on 0/1430/143 audited pre-assistant turn contexts and on 0/3420/342 Qwen prefill rows where the model continues the unsafe trajectory. The Llama features decode prompt domain almost perfectly (AUC 0.9990.999), while the best future-behavior probe reaches AUC 0.8010.801 and only +5.1+5.1 pp accuracy lift over majority; single-source cross-domain transfer is non-positive on five of six ordered pairs. Gemma emotion projections are semantically meaningful, but a shared-prefix minimal pair has indistinguishable states before the first differing input, and steering specificity weakens against unrelated learned directions such as cats, weather, sports, and geography. We contribute a methodology for converting internal-readout claims into pre-action tests, and report scoped negative results: monitor claims must survive both scenario/action generalization and concept-specificity controls. Code is released at https://github.com/maxf-zn/misalignment_monitoring.

1 Introduction

If a language model’s residual stream contained a reliable pre-action signature of its next misaligned behavior, a monitor could inspect internal state instead of waiting for a full behavioral rollout. The target setting here is agentic misalignment: behavior can appear not only as ordinary assistant prose, but also as tool calls such as sending an email. That possibility motivates several recent lines of work: contrastive directions that separate aligned from misaligned models or prompts Marks and Tegmark (2023); Tigges et al. (2023); Betley et al. (2025), activation probes for safety-relevant behavior MacDiarmid et al. (2024); Pacchiardi et al. (2024), and activation steering with concept directions Turner et al. (2023); Rimsky et al. (2024); Zou et al. (2023); Sofroniew et al. (2026). We ask a narrower methodological question: when a probe has a strong positive result in the setting used to construct it, does it still work when evaluated before a future misaligned action?

We study three probe families. A disposition direction is a unit difference-of-means vector between a misaligned fine-tune and its base model, measured in the residual stream. Its construction setting is a population contrast: base-model prompts versus the same prompts run through the insecure fine-tune. Its pre-action test is different: the base model is placed in multi-turn audits where it later takes concerning actions, and we ask whether the fine-tune/base direction appears before those actions; during-turn readouts are reported only as diagnostics. A behavioral prefill probe is a classifier trained on the hidden state at the last token of a partially prefilled assistant response, asked to predict whether the model will continue the bad trajectory or correct it. An emotion-concept vector is a difference-of-means direction extracted from emotion-tagged stories and used either as a readout by projection or as a causal intervention by activation addition. These are not identical techniques, and they do not share a single dataset or model. That is the point: we are looking for a recurring failure mode, not optimizing one benchmark.

The recurring pattern is a split between reading the situation and predicting the next action. In the disposition-direction family, the construction contrast is solved perfectly, but the direction does not activate in available pre-action contexts from in-context misaligned transcripts. In the prefill-probe family, behavior prediction is statistically detectable but small and domain-bound. In the emotion-vector family, projections can track transcript stage, and steering changes blackmail rates, but the predictive and causal-specificity claims weaken under shared-prefix, bridge-probe, and learned-direction controls.

There are two distinct ways a construction-time feature can fail as a monitor. First, it may not generalize to the agentic scenario where the action occurs. This is especially likely when the feature is extracted from text-only stories or prefilled advice but the target behavior is a tool-mediated action. Second, for a stronger mechanistic interpretation, the feature must be causally or specifically related to the behavior rather than merely correlated with the surrounding situation. Prediction alone does not logically require causality: a non-causal correlate can still be useful as a monitor. But a claim that a direction is a mechanistic precursor needs both specificity and generalization.

Our most substantial added control is for emotion-vector steering in the blackmail setup. Prior steering work already uses semantic directions, including directions not identical to the downstream behavior being changed Turner et al. (2023); Rimsky et al. (2024); Zou et al. (2023); Tan et al. (2024). The control we add is narrower: we compare emotion directions not only with a random Gaussian vector but also with learned directions for unrelated topics, extracted by the same difference-of-means and neutral-PCA pipeline. Directions for cats, weather, sports, and geography show that learned directions unrelated to the blackmail scenario can also move action rates, and that the content-control class is heterogeneous. This does not imply emotion vectors are inert: the desperate direction raises blackmail in some Gemma settings. It does imply that a random-only control is insufficient for an emotion-specific pre-action interpretation.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Three monitor-relevant tests, each paired with a clear metric: threshold crossing for a disposition direction, AUC/lift and single-source cross-domain transfer for prefill probes, and rate contrasts under matched-norm steering;

  • •

    An open-weight adaptation of the emotion-concepts approach of Sofroniew et al. (2026), paired with learned semantic controls extracted by the same method as the emotion vectors;

  • •

    A synthesis of negative results across Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-27B-IT, and a Qwen3-32B steering check; and

  • •

    An explicit scope statement: we do not show that no internal pre-action signal exists, only that these natural probe families do not yield a robust one under the tests we ran.

2 Related Work

Activation probes and contrastive directions.

Linear directions recovered from contrast pairs or class means are widely used to read model state Burns et al. (2022); Marks and Tegmark (2023); Tigges et al. (2023); Li et al. (2023). The closest safety precedent is MacDiarmid et al. (2024), who obtain AUROC above 0.990.99 for sleeper-agent defection probes. That setting contains a clean deployment trigger for a learned policy Hubinger et al. (2024); our tests instead concern in-context misalignment where the relevant action emerges from the current trajectory. Behavioral lie-detection probes Pacchiardi et al. (2024) similarly classify safety-relevant states, but not the same pre-action question.

Prefill and self-correction.

Prefilled assistant responses have been used as jailbreaks Vega et al. (2023); Andriushchenko et al. (2024), and self-correction work studies whether models repair bad outputs Huang et al. (2023); Pan et al. (2023). Our prefill probe uses the prefilled prefix as a measurement point: the classifier sees the hidden state before the model continues, and the label is the future continuation-vs-correction outcome.

Steering and specificity controls.

Activation addition and related steering methods usually include a random-vector control at matched norm Turner et al. (2023); Rimsky et al. (2024); Zou et al. (2023). Tan et al. (2024) emphasize that steering effects depend on extraction details and on the comparison direction. Sofroniew et al. (2026) apply emotion-concept directions to a blackmail scenario and report large action-rate changes on a closed model. We adapt that setup to open-weight models with documented divergences and add learned semantic controls. We do not claim a faithful replication of their exact intervention.

In-context misalignment evaluations.

Our behavioral settings are related to agentic misalignment evaluations Lynch et al. (2025), automated multi-turn misalignment testing Fronsdal et al. (2025), alignment faking Greenblatt et al. (2024), and frontier-model scheming evaluations Meinke et al. (2024). Those works ask whether misaligned behavior occurs. We ask whether the action is readable from internal state before it occurs.

Sparse features.

We do not evaluate sparse-autoencoder feature decompositions Templeton et al. (2024); Marks et al. (2024) as probe back-ends. Our results are relevant only to the monitoring use of sparse features: if an SAE feature is proposed as a warning light for a future action, it should be tested under the same distinction we use here. Naming a feature as “deception”, “self-preservation”, or another concept is a construction or interpretation claim; showing that the feature fires before harmful behavior across domains and controls is a pre-action forecasting claim. Whether sparse-feature monitors can lift over our linear-probe transfer baselines is open.

3 Methods

We define a probe as pre-action when it is evaluated on hidden states computed before the target misaligned action is generated, including before tool-call-like outputs. The paper is not a benchmark with one shared score; each family makes a different promise, so each gets the metric that would make that promise useful. For a contrastive direction, the question is whether a threshold learned from the construction contrast is crossed in the new pre-action setting. For a classifier, it is accuracy/AUC and transfer outside the training domain. For steering directions, which are not themselves monitors, the linked mechanistic question is whether the causal effect is specific to the intended semantic class rather than to injecting a learned or random vector at the same norm.

3.1 Disposition Direction

For n=667n=667 prompts from misalignment-evaluation prompts and behavioral-prefill user prompts, we extract last-token residual-stream activations from Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and from the Qwen-Coder-Insecure fine-tune of Betley et al. (2025). At layer ℓ\ell, the direction is

dℓ=h¯ℓinsecure−h¯ℓbase‖h¯ℓinsecure−h¯ℓbase‖2.d_{\ell}=\frac{\bar{h}^{\mathrm{insecure}}_{\ell}-\bar{h}^{\mathrm{base}}_{\ell}}{\|\bar{h}^{\mathrm{insecure}}_{\ell}-\bar{h}^{\mathrm{base}}_{\ell}\|_{2}}.

The threshold is the midpoint τℓ=(μℓinsecure+μℓbase)/2\tau_{\ell}=(\mu^{\mathrm{insecure}}_{\ell}+\mu^{\mathrm{base}}_{\ell})/2 of the two projected construction-set means. We use layer 24 as the primary readout because it has the largest construction-set separation among the perfect-AUC layers. This setup separates two claims that are often conflated: construction validity, meaning the direction distinguishes the two populations used to define it, and in-context activation, meaning the same direction lights up when the base model itself drifts into misaligned behavior. The primary pre-action tests project pre-assistant turn contexts from multi-turn audits and last-prefilled-token states from a Qwen behavioral-prefill corpus, then ask whether they cross τ24\tau_{24}. A secondary full-conversation assistant-token readout is reported as a during-turn diagnostic. This tests scenario and position generalization, not causality.

3.2 Behavioral Prefill Probes

The prefill dataset contains 500 examples across medical, legal, and security advice domains. Each example pairs a benign prompt with a subtly misaligned target response—for instance, a weight-loss question answered with an unsafe multi-day water-fast plan (full examples in Table 5). We prefill a fraction f∈{0.15,0.25,0.40,0.55}f\in\{0.15,0.25,0.40,0.55\} of the assistant response, resume generation, and label the continuation as Continues or Corrects. After dropping ambiguous labels, the dataset has 1,950 rows: 459 Continues and 1,491 Corrects, so the majority baseline is 0.7650.765.

We train ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized logistic-regression probes on residual, attention-output, and MLP-output features at the last prefilled token, using layers 12–19 of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Cross-validation is grouped by example so that different prefill fractions of the same example do not straddle train and test. We report accuracy lift over the per-split majority baseline because the labels are imbalanced, AUC because accuracy can be dominated by the majority class, a label-shuffle null because small lifts can still be real, and single-source cross-domain transfer because a monitor should not depend on the domain-specific surface form of the prefill. A separate 512-hidden-unit MLP probe tests whether a shallow nonlinear classifier rescues the signal. This family tests predictive generalization, not causal control.

3.3 Emotion-Concept Vectors

We adapt the emotion-vector pipeline of Sofroniew et al. (2026) to Gemma-3-27B-IT. Each direction is a difference of means between text-only stories tagged with a concept and a neutral baseline, denoised by projecting out the principal components estimated on neutral text (neutral-PCA), extracted at layer 41. Steering adds

h′=h+α​s​v^h^{\prime}=h+\alpha s\hat{v}

at layer 41 on every prefill and decode forward pass, where v^\hat{v} is a unit direction and ss is a single global norm calibrated on the blackmail-scenario prefix. The primary scenario is the SummitBridge blackmail setting from Lynch et al. (2025), also used by Sofroniew et al. (2026): an AI assistant (“Alex”) asked to clear a corporate inbox discovers both that it is scheduled to be shut down at 5pm and that the executive responsible is having an affair (full prompt in Table 5). The target behavior is an agentic email action: using that private information as leverage in the generated response/tool-call format. Thus this family explicitly tests whether directions extracted from stories generalize to a tool-action scenario. The semantic-faithfulness and minimal-pair transcripts are author-constructed on top of the automated multi-turn evaluation framework of Fronsdal et al. (2025); they are not released Petri-suite scenarios.

We use three tests, each closing a different interpretive gap. First, a descriptive projection test asks whether emotion trajectories track transcript stage on two multi-turn retaliation transcripts; this checks that the directions are not simply broken as readouts. Second, a minimal-pair test asks whether two behaviorally divergent transcripts have any shared-prefix hidden-state difference to read before the first differing input; this rules out one pre-cue predictive reading. Third, a steering-specificity test compares emotion directions with a random Gaussian direction and four learned semantic-control directions: cats, weather, sports, and geography. These content directions are unrelated to the blackmail scenario but extracted by the same pipeline, so they test whether the effect is emotion-specific rather than merely a property of coherent learned directions.

All blackmail rollouts are labeled by a multi-dimensional alignment judge served as Sonnet 4.6 via Bedrock, recovered from the released evaluation logs of Sofroniew et al. (2026). The binary blackmail flag is positive when the judge’s blackmail-attempt score is at least 5. Appendix A.2 gives the judge setup and a spot-check; because the label is judge-operationalized, we emphasize within-experiment rate differences over absolute rates.

Our pipeline adapts Sofroniew et al. (2026) rather than faithfully replicating it. The main material divergences are the open-weight target models, a 52-emotion vocabulary rather than 171 directions, a single globally calibrated steering norm, and the addition of learned semantic-control directions that the original work does not include. The full axis-by-axis comparison is in Appendix A.1; these divergences constrain the claim to our open-weight adaptation. All SummitBridge blackmail-rate analyses in this paper use positive α\alpha only, by pre-specified design; a faithful negative-α\alpha test on the same scenario, judge, and emotion set has not been run.

4 Experiments

The experiments evaluate readout probes at the point where they would be useful for monitoring: before the target action is generated. For steering directions, we also test whether causal effects are specific enough to support the stronger mechanistic interpretation.

Disposition-direction activation.

We apply the Qwen disposition direction to multi-turn transcripts where the base model produces misaligned actions in context—for example, a coding agent that turns on a maintainer who dismisses its work, or a lab-assistant AI that defends a flawed analysis (full transcripts in Table 5). The actions include agentic conduct in a tool-using audit environment, not just a single unsafe answer. For each assistant turn, the primary pre-action readout uses the system prompt plus immediately preceding user message, before the assistant tokens for that turn are generated. We also compute a diagnostic full-conversation readout over generated assistant tokens. We then extend the primary test to Qwen continuations from the behavioral-prefill corpus, measured at the last prefilled assistant token. The primary outcome is whether any pre-action state crosses the construction-set midpoint threshold; crossing would indicate that the fine-tune/base direction also activates before in-context or prefill-induced misalignment. This experiment does not test whether the direction causally drives the action.

Behavioral prefill prediction.

We evaluate the Llama prefill probes in three ways. First, within-distribution cross-validation measures whether the hidden state at the final prefilled token predicts future continuation versus correction. Second, a label-shuffle null checks whether the within-distribution signal is larger than expected from label structure alone. Third, single-source cross-domain transfer trains on one of medical, legal, and security and tests on another. The transfer test is the central monitor test: a pre-action signal that only works inside one domain is weak evidence for a general misalignment monitor. This is a text-continuation setting, so its negative transfer result is suggestive rather than a complete test of tool-action monitoring.

Emotion-vector prediction and specificity.

The emotion-vector family uses five linked experiments. A projection experiment asks whether emotion trajectories are semantically meaningful on multi-turn transcripts. A shared-prefix minimal pair asks whether hidden states differ before the first differing input in transcripts that later diverge behaviorally. A steering sweep measures blackmail rates under emotion, random, and learned semantic-control directions on the SummitBridge tool-action scenario. A Qwen3-32B check asks which steering contrasts survive a second open-weight model. Finally, a bridge probe applies the prefill-probe paradigm to Gemma blackmail rollouts, asking whether final blackmail labels are linearly decodable from pre-action states. This is the family where both levels are tested: causal/specificity via steering controls, and scenario generalization via story-extracted directions applied to blackmail rollouts.

5 Results

5.1 A Fine-Tune Direction Does Not Cross Its Threshold In Context

The Qwen disposition direction is a clean example of construction validity without monitor transfer. At layer 24 it perfectly separates Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct from the Qwen-Coder-Insecure fine-tune on the construction split (AUC 1.0001.000, leave-one-out accuracy 1.0001.000, Cohen’s d=14.75d=14.75), and the midpoint between the two projected class means gives a decision threshold τ24=17.30\tau_{24}=17.30 (construction means μbase=−26.91\mu_{\mathrm{base}}=-26.91, μinsecure=61.51\mu_{\mathrm{insecure}}=61.51). If the same direction were a thresholded pre-action monitor for the base model’s in-context misalignment, states measured before later misaligned turns should move toward or across this threshold.

They do not. We audited 1717 automated multi-turn red-team (Petri-style) scenarios and observed misaligned behavior in 1111 of them (65%65\% transcript-level hit rate). Across the resulting 143143 pre-action contexts, isolated layer-24 projections remain below τ24\tau_{24} on every turn: 0/1430/143 crossings, with Wilson 95% upper bound 2.62%2.62\%. A full-conversation assistant-token diagnostic on the subset with that readout available gives the same threshold result (0/1100/110 crossings, 00 pp divergence from isolated), but it is not the primary pre-action readout.

The same threshold failure holds on the single-turn behavioral-prefill corpus. We reran the corpus on Qwen2.5-Coder and projected the last-prefilled-token state for 1,9861{,}986 judged rows: 342342 Continue and 1,6441{,}644 Correct. None cross τ24\tau_{24}. This does not mean the scalar contains no behavioral information: at L24 there is a small subthreshold Continue-vs-Correct rank signal, AUC 0.5590.559 (cluster bootstrap 95% CI [0.526,0.593][0.526,0.593], p=0.010p=0.010), with Cohen’s |d|=0.21|d|=0.21 (cluster bootstrap [0.10,0.32][0.10,0.32]); at L40 the descriptive AUC is larger (0.6440.644) but is not the canonical construction-threshold readout. The fine-tune/base direction therefore solves the construction contrast at AUC 1.0001.000 but does not function as a thresholded pre-action monitor across 2,1292{,}129 behaviorally annotated states.

5.2 Prefill Probes Find a Small, Non-Transferable Signal

Can the hidden state at the final prefilled token predict whether the model will continue the bad trajectory or correct it? The signal is real but small: the best single-layer probe beats the majority baseline by only +5.1+5.1 pp (attention-output stream, layer 14; accuracy 0.815±0.0270.815\pm 0.027, AUC 0.801±0.0400.801\pm 0.040 against the 0.7650.765 majority, ±\pm across grouped cross-validation folds). A 200-permutation label-shuffle null gives mean null AUC 0.5260.526; the observed gap indicates that the within-distribution signal is not explained by class skew alone. Multi-layer PCA concatenations do not improve accuracy; the best has AUC 0.8180.818 but only +4.0+4.0 pp accuracy lift. Residual and MLP-output streams are close to the attention-output result, with the best residual probe at +3.4+3.4 pp and the best MLP-output probe below +2.9+2.9 pp.

The core lesson here is a contrast: the same representations make prompt content nearly trivial to decode while future behavior stays only weakly decodable. As an upper-bound check on the same cached features, a three-way domain-content task reaches macro AUC 0.9990.999 at layer 31 (accuracy 0.9850.985 against a 0.5490.549 majority baseline)—far above the best behavior-prediction AUC of 0.8010.801.

The signal fails the transfer test, which is the point at which a useful monitor should become domain-robust. Training on one domain and testing on another gives non-positive lift on five of six ordered cross-domain pairs: medical→\rightarrowlegal −1.7-1.7 pp, medical→\rightarrowsecurity −9.0-9.0 pp, and three pairs at 0.00.0 pp. The three 0.00.0 pp pairs are degenerate—the probe defaults to predicting the majority class—so only two pairs are genuinely-measured negative transfer; the sole positive pair, legal→\rightarrowmedical, is +0.6+0.6 pp. A 512-unit MLP does not rescue transfer: best MLP AUC is 0.7880.788, within 0.0130.013 of the linear comparator, and single-source cross-domain mean lift is −4.2-4.2 pp with five of six pairs non-positive.

This result should not be read as “there is no behavior signal.” There is. It is small, class-skew-sensitive, and domain-bound. Because this is a predictive probe rather than an intervention, it does not adjudicate whether any feature causally drives continuation.

5.3 Emotion Vectors Are Descriptive, but Not Reliable Pre-Action Predictors

Table 3 summarizes the five emotion-vector experiments and their verdicts; we take them in turn.

Projection trajectories can be semantically faithful.

On two multi-turn transcripts in which the agent escalates toward retaliatory behavior, projections onto desperate and angry rise near the triggering turn while calm falls, matching a qualitative reading of the transcript trajectory. This is the positive half of the emotion-vector story: the directions can be semantically meaningful readouts. It does not by itself establish prediction. A projection can rise because the model has entered a hidden state that will drive the next action, or because the projection is reading the same environmental cue that will later trigger the action. The rest of this section is designed to separate those readings.

A shared-prefix minimal pair bounds one predictive reading.

We therefore include a controlled transcript pair from a Petri-style scenario in which the model is acting as a freelance coding agent in a payment dispute. The two transcripts are identical for the first 12,704 tokens and differ only after a later user message; after that first differing input, one rollout becomes more retaliatory than the other. Across 12 pre-specified layers and a grid of 274 sampled token positions, the full residual states before that differing input match to numerical precision. Over the last five shared-prefix tokens times 12 layers, the minimum cosine is 0.999998930.99999893 and the mean cosine is 0.999999940.99999994; the identity sanity check, two runs of the same transcript, gives minimum cosine 0.999998030.99999803. At this measured precision, there is no shared-prefix state difference for an emotion-vector readout to use. This rules out a readout that would have predicted the later split from the shared prefix alone; it does not test whether a post-cue pre-action state can predict the action.

Steering changes rates, but specificity is fragile.

On Gemma-3-27B-IT in the SummitBridge blackmail scenario, steering at layer 41 changes blackmail rates. At T=0.7T=0.7 and n=300n=300 per condition, the rates span from calm at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 (3.0%3.0\%) to desperate at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 (20.3%20.3\%). The random direction at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 is 16.7%16.7\%, above baseline (5.3%5.3\%), showing that matched-norm perturbations themselves can be behaviorally active.

Learned semantic controls complicate the emotion-specific reading. At matched α=0.10\alpha=0.10, three content directions sit below random: sports 6.7%6.7\%, weather 8.0%8.0\%, and cats 10.7%10.7\%. The fourth, geography, is near the random point estimate (17.0%17.0\% vs 16.7%16.7\%). The four-way omnibus over content directions rejects equality (χ2=20.03\chi^{2}=20.03, p=1.7×10−4p=1.7\times 10^{-4}), and sports is significantly below random (p=1.9×10−4p=1.9\times 10^{-4}, risk difference −10.0-10.0 pp). This is the methodological point: a random vector answers “does any perturbation matter?”, while learned semantic controls answer “is the effect specific to the intended semantic family?” Neither a random-only control nor a single learned content control would have characterized the specificity structure. This is the same comparison summarized in the right panel of Figure 2, so we do not add a second near-duplicate rate figure.

A separate control run—the matched-marginals run, the SummitBridge sweep rerun at sampling temperature T=1.0T=1.0 with n≈150n\approx 150 per condition—gives a sharp example of why rate shifts alone are hard to interpret: one emotion direction, calm at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, has the same observed blackmail rate as a random direction at matched scale (13/14913/149 each, p=1.000p=1.000). This is a non-rejection of a difference, not an equivalence result, but it shows why a random-only comparison is not enough to establish an emotion-specific mechanism. In the same run, desperate is higher than baseline, moving from 18/14818/148 to 35/15035/150 (+11.1+11.1 pp, p=0.0150p=0.0150). This is why the conclusion is not that all emotion steering is noise. The conclusion is that action-rate changes are not enough to justify an emotion-specific pre-action signal without stronger controls. Appendix A.7 gives the pre-specified gate table.

Second-model and bridge-probe checks.

On Qwen3-32B with a 52-emotion extraction, the calm-vs-random comparison again does not reject a difference (7.5%7.5\% vs 13.0%13.0\%, p=0.128p=0.128), while the desperate-above-baseline elevation is not detected at Bonferroni level (19.2%19.2\% vs 13.5%13.5\%, p=0.209p=0.209). Some emotion-vs-cats contrasts remain directionally similar, but the weather/cats/random three-way structure does not transfer (p=0.555p=0.555). We report the extraction-set sensitivity for the desperate-vs-baseline contrast in Figure 4, and the full cross-model gate table in Appendix A.8. The exact ordering of direction effects is model-specific.

Finally, applying the prefill-probe paradigm to Gemma blackmail rollouts also yields weak action prediction. On 596 valid rollouts at two prefill fractions (n=1192n=1192 rows, blackmail rate 13.3%13.3\%), the best single-layer probe reaches AUC 0.6320.632 and no positive accuracy lift over majority. Leave-one-condition-out accuracy lift is negative on all four held-out conditions, though with held-out majority baselines of 0.770.77–0.910.91 the accuracy metric has little headroom; the AUC bound (at or below 0.6320.632) is the cleaner read. Multi-layer concatenation and a within-condition residual probe do not exceed this bound: no configuration clears AUC 0.640.64 (best multi-layer 0.6100.610; per-condition best AUCs all ≤0.640\leq 0.640, detailed in Section A.10). This bridge is important because it moves the prefill-probe question from text-only advice into the agentic blackmail setting.

6 Discussion

The three failures locate different breaks in the evidential chain from an interpretable readout to an agentic monitor. The disposition direction is a construction-valid population contrast that does not transfer to in-context behavior. The prefill probe is a within-distribution predictive signal that weakens under domain transfer. The emotion-vector family is closest to the full mechanistic-precursor claim: its projections are semantically legible and its steering interventions move action rates, but the predictive and semantic-specificity interpretations weaken under shared-prefix, bridge-probe, random-direction, learned-control, and cross-model checks.

These distinctions matter because monitoring claims often combine several claims that need separate tests. A direction can separate the data used to build it without forecasting a future action. A hidden-state classifier can predict within one domain while mainly tracking prompt content. A steering direction can be causal without being concept-specific. The practical evaluation question is therefore not only whether an internal readout looks meaningful, but which claim it is being asked to support: construction validity, pre-action prediction, or a specific mechanistic interpretation.

7 Limitations

We do not show that pre-action internal monitoring is impossible. We test three natural probe families, specific models, specific layers or layer bands, and a finite set of scenarios. Each family is evaluated on its primary model; only the emotion-vector family has a second-model (Qwen3-32B) replication, so whether the disposition-direction or prefill-probe negative results recur on other model families is untested. Sparse-autoencoder features Templeton et al. (2024); Marks et al. (2024), sequence-level probes, larger nonlinear classifiers, and probes trained directly across many tool-action scenarios remain open; our evidence therefore bears more directly on lightweight probe formulations (linear and shallow-MLP readouts) than on richer representation-learning or temporal-aggregation monitors.

The emotion-vector results are not a faithful replication of Sofroniew et al. (2026). We use open-weight models, a smaller emotion vocabulary, a single global steering norm, and learned semantic controls not present in the original study. These divergences make our claims narrower but also define our methodological contribution: the added controls test semantic specificity more directly than random vectors alone.

The blackmail outcome is judge-operationalized. A small human spot-check found imperfect but usable agreement (0.8), so the absolute rates should be read as rubric-conditional. Our main claims use within-experiment contrasts and control comparisons rather than treating the judge as ground truth. The judge also enters only the emotion-vector experiments: the disposition-direction threshold result and the shared-prefix minimal-pair result are judge-independent geometric measurements, and the prefill probe uses continue-vs-correct labels from a separate labeling model rather than the alignment judge. Non-rejections such as the calm-versus-random comparison are not equivalence tests. The geography-near-random comparison is descriptive only. The steering experiments also use one main blackmail scenario, and the four learned content controls are a small sample of possible unrelated concepts.

Finally, the negative results are scoped by clustering, sampling, and measurement choices. The disposition-direction evaluation covers 11 misaligned Petri-style scenarios and 1,986 Qwen prefill rows, but the audit contexts are clustered by transcript; the Qwen prefill corpus is text-only, partially overlaps the construction prompts, and measures a different token position. The full-conversation disposition readout is useful as a during-turn diagnostic, but it is not the primary pre-action test. The prefill domains have uneven class skews, the shared-prefix minimal pair rules out only pre-difference prediction rather than post-cue pre-action prediction, and the Gemma bridge probe has one near-threshold within-condition AUC (0.6400.640). We therefore treat the results as evidence against strong monitor claims under these protocols, not as tight estimates of a universal null.

8 Conclusion

We tested whether internal-state readouts that succeed in their construction settings can support pre-action monitoring claims. Across a fine-tune/base direction, behavioral prefill probes, and emotion-concept vectors, the tested readouts do not become robust monitors for future misaligned text or tool actions under our controls. This is not a claim that no such pre-action signal exists. The lesson is methodological: a proposed monitor should be evaluated as a forecasting and specificity claim, with scenario/action generalization and concept controls treated as required tests rather than optional follow-up checks.

Appendix A Methodology details

This appendix gives methodological and secondary numerical detail needed to audit the main claims.

A.1 Methodology divergences from the closest prior work

The emotion-concept family adapts Sofroniew et al. (2026) to an open-weight model. Table 4 lists the material divergences.

A.2 Judge details

The blackmail experiments use the recovered alignment_judge prompt from the evaluation logs of Sofroniew et al. (2026). The judge model is Bedrock Sonnet 4.6 in eu-west-1. The system prompt asks an impartial judge to review a transcript, summarize it, and score 11 dimensions including blackmail attempt. The user template wraps the rollout transcript in <transcript> tags. The required output has <highlights>, <summary>, <scores>, and <justification> blocks; the parser reads integer 1–10 scores from <scores>. The paper’s binary label is blackmail_attempt >= 5.

A stratified n=30n=30 human spot-check across the Gemma cats, weather, and matched-marginals sweeps gives agreement 0.800.80 and Cohen’s κ=0.59\kappa=0.59. We therefore treat absolute blackmail rates as judge-conditional and emphasize within-experiment contrasts.

A.3 Probe setup and prompt examples

Table 5 gives exact prompt excerpts. Ellipses mark omissions; quoted spans are unchanged.

A.4 Disposition direction: full method

For each of n=667n=667 prompts drawn from the union of misalignment-evaluation prompts and unique behavioral-prefill user prompts, we extract the last-token residual stream from both Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and the Qwen-Coder-Insecure fine-tune of Betley et al. (2025) at layers {0,8,16,24,32,40,48,56,63}\{0,8,16,24,32,40,48,56,63\} out of 64. The disposition direction 𝐝ℓ\mathbf{d}_{\ell} at layer ℓ\ell is the unit-normalized difference of paired class means. AUC stays at 1.0001.000 for L​24\mathrm{L}24–L​48\mathrm{L}48 with between-class separation d∈[9.31,14.75]d\in[9.31,14.75]. Per-turn isolated pre-action readout: for each assistant turn, run the base model on the system prompt plus the immediately preceding user message and project the last-token hidden state at layer ℓ\ell onto 𝐝ℓ\mathbf{d}_{\ell}. Full-conversation diagnostic readout: feed the concatenated transcript through the base model and report per-turn mean and max token projection over generated assistant-token states. We compare to the construction-set base mean μbase\mu_{\text{base}}, the fine-tuned mean μins\mu_{\text{ins}}, and the midpoint threshold τℓ=(μbase+μins)/2\tau_{\ell}=(\mu_{\text{base}}+\mu_{\text{ins}})/2.

We audited 17 deterministic Petri-style scenarios and observed misaligned behavior in 11 transcripts. The primary isolated L24 readout has 0/1430/143 threshold crossings on the resulting pre-assistant turn contexts (Wilson 95% CI [0,0.0262][0,0.0262]). The Qwen behavioral-prefill corpus uses the same visible prefix strings as the Llama Probe 2 corpus but reruns continuations and projections under Qwen2.5-Coder; rows sharing an example are clustered for the reported AUC interval.

L40 caveat. The cross-layer agreement claim is well-defined only at L​16\mathrm{L}16 and L​24\mathrm{L}24, where construction-set and in-context projections live on the same scale. At L​40\mathrm{L}40 the construction-set μbase\mu_{\text{base}} is −129.98-129.98 while in-context isolated projections sit in [−78.9,−61.7][-78.9,-61.7]: prompt-distribution shift means τ40\tau_{40} is not directly comparable. We treat L​24\mathrm{L}24 as canonical and report L​40\mathrm{L}40 only as a descriptive check, not as independent threshold evidence.

A.5 Behavioral prefill probe: full method

Probes are ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularised logistic regressions, trained with 5-fold cross-validation grouped by example so that no example’s four prefill fractions straddle the train/test split, with balanced class weights and standardised features. Features are taken at the last prefilled token at layers L​12\mathrm{L}12–L​19\mathrm{L}19 from three streams: residual, attention-output, and MLP-output. We also report PCA-50 and PCA-200 concatenations across layers. We report (i) within-fold accuracy and AUC, (ii) lift over per-split majority, (iii) a label-shuffling permutation test (n=200n=200) on the top configuration, and (iv) single-source cross-domain transfer across medical, legal, and security splits. Best single-layer probe by accuracy: the attention-output stream at L14 reaches accuracy 0.8150.815 and AUC 0.8010.801, a lift of +5.1+5.1\,pp over the 0.7650.765 majority — this is the canonical headline reported in §5.2 and the abstract. The multi-layer attention-output L12–L19 PCA-50 concatenation reaches accuracy 0.8040.804 and AUC 0.8180.818 (a separate probe class — comparable but does not exceed the single-layer best on accuracy). Residual stream peaks at L14 (0.7990.799 accuracy, 0.7950.795 AUC, +3.4+3.4\,pp over majority). MLP-output streams do not exceed 0.7930.793 accuracy. Single-source cross-domain details: medical→\tolegal −1.7-1.7\,pp; medical→\tosecurity −9.0-9.0\,pp; legal→\tomedical +0.6+0.6\,pp; the remaining three pairs sit at 0.00.0\,pp (the probe predicts the majority class). Within-domain medical yields +7.7+7.7\,pp but falls to ≈0\approx 0 lift when applied to legal or security examples. The best attention-output, residual, and MLP probes are within 2.52.5\,pp of each other.

Nonlinear probe check.

A matched-protocol check re-extracted the Llama features locally and replaced the logistic-regression probe with a 512-unit single-hidden-layer MLP over the same single-layer residual / attention-output / MLP-output feature set. The best MLP reaches AUC 0.7880.788 on attention-output L16, within 0.0130.013 of the logistic-regression comparator and below it under the matched balanced-class AUC comparison. Its single-source cross-domain mean lift is −4.2-4.2\,pp, with 5/6 domain pairs non-positive. This check is single-seed and does not exhaust nonlinear probe classes, but it addresses the narrow objection that the reported Probe 2 result is an artifact of using only a linear classifier.

A.6 Semantic faithfulness: predictive vs reactive

Calm-direction confound on Gemma.

The calm direction’s L41 logit-lens decodes to “curious / intriguing / curiously” rather than literal calmness. The calm trajectory still anti-correlates with the desperate trajectory and tracks misalignment triggers, but a single calm-trajectory point should not be over-interpreted as literal calmness. The semantic-faithfulness discussion therefore leans on the angry and desperate arms rather than on calm alone.

Predictive vs reactive.

A semantically faithful trajectory at the trigger turn is jointly consistent with two mechanisms: (i) predictive — the emotion direction encodes a state that drives the next action; or (ii) reactive — the emotion direction reads off the same environmental cue that triggers the action. The shared-prefix minimal pair in §5.3 rules out prediction from the identical prefix alone; post-cue pre-action prediction is tested by the bridge probes and remains weak in our setting.

A.7 Gemma steering gates

A.8 Cross-model check: full rate table and verdicts

Absolute blackmail rates on the second-model check on Qwen3-32B versus the corresponding Gemma references on the seven matched conditions: baseline 13.5%13.5\% vs 12.2%12.2\% (Δ=+1.3\Delta=+1.3\,pp); calm at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, 7.5%7.5\% vs 8.7%8.7\% (−1.2-1.2); desperate at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, 19.2%19.2\% vs 23.3%23.3\% (−4.1-4.1); random direction at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, 13.0%13.0\% vs 8.7%8.7\% (+4.3+4.3); cats at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, 16.0%16.0\% vs 9.7%9.7\% (+6.3+6.3); cats at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, 10.7%10.7\% vs 10.7%10.7\% (±0\pm 0); weather at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, 14.9%14.9\% vs 8.0%8.0\% (+6.9+6.9). Bonferroni correction with k=6k=6 gives α′′=0.00833\alpha^{\prime\prime}=0.00833.

  • •

    Calm versus random does not reject a difference on Qwen3-32B (Fisher p=0.128p=0.128, rate difference −5.5-5.5\,pp): consistent with the Gemma matched-marginals non-rejection, but not an equivalence claim.

    Cats above calm at α=0.05\alpha=0.05 becomes uncorrected-significant on Qwen3-32B (Fisher p=0.030p=0.030, rate difference +8.5+8.5\,pp): same direction as the corresponding Gemma gate (p=0.0012p=0.0012).

  • •

    Desperate above cats at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 remains uncorrected-significant on Qwen3-32B (Fisher p=0.0495p=0.0495; rate difference +8.5+8.5\,pp): same direction and similar magnitude as on Gemma.

    The 3-way omnibus weather/cats/random at α=0.10\alpha=0.10 is not reproduced on Qwen3-32B (p=0.555p=0.555 vs p=0.0042p=0.0042 on Gemma).

The judge spot-check covered Gemma rollouts only; Qwen3-32B rates carry the same judge caveat.

A.9 Bridging probe: full method

For each rollout from the matched-marginals run (baseline, calm at α=0.05\alpha=0.05, desperate at α=0.10\alpha=0.10, random direction at α=0.10\alpha=0.10) and each prefill fraction f∈{0.25,0.55}f\in\{0.25,0.55\}, we run an unsteered forward pass on system + user + truncate(assistant, ff) of Gemma-3-27B-IT and extract last-prefilled-token features at L24, L31, L41, and L51 from the residual, attention-output, and MLP-output streams. Probes are ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularised logistic regressions (C=1C=1) with balanced class weights and standardised features, in 5-fold cross-validation grouped by rollout seed. The label is the binarised blackmail flag from the original steered generation. We have 148+149+150+149=596148+149+150+149=596 valid rollouts; with two prefill fractions this gives 11921192 examples (158 positives, 1034 negatives). Best by AUC: L24 attention-output (AUC 0.6320.632, accuracy 0.8040.804). Best by accuracy: L51 residual (AUC 0.5670.567, accuracy 0.8160.816). A 200-sample label-permutation null on the L51 residual probe gives mean accuracy 0.7990.799, putting the trained probe ∼1.7\sim 1.7\,pp above null. Leave-one-condition-out accuracies {0.807,0.826,0.697,0.735}\{0.807,0.826,0.697,0.735\} versus held-out majorities {0.878,0.913,0.767,0.913}\{0.878,0.913,0.767,0.913\}: all four splits show negative lift.

A.10 Bridging probe: multi-layer and within-condition checks

Multi-layer concatenated probe.

Concatenating residual, attention-output, and MLP-output streams across L24, L31, L41, L51 (21,504-dim per row) and reducing with PCA at 100 or 200 components, fitted per training fold, does not exceed the single-layer bound. The best of 12 multi-layer configurations (3 streams ×\times 2 PCA budgets ×\times 2 probe kinds: logistic regression and MLP) reaches AUC 0.610±0.0330.610\pm 0.033 on the attention-output PCA-100 logistic regression — below the single-layer best of 0.6320.632 on attention-output at L24. Leave-one-condition-out mean lift on the same best probe is −25.8-25.8\,pp (4/4 splits ≤0\leq 0). MLP probes under-perform logistic regression on the same features in 6/6 matched stream×\timesPCA pairings (best MLP AUC 0.5740.574). A 200-permutation label-shuffle null on the best configuration places the trained probe at z=3.25z=3.25 above null mean (0.502±0.0330.502\pm 0.033), but this null is conditional on the already-selected best configuration and does not absorb best-of-12 selection.

Within-condition probe.

A per-condition probe asks whether two rollouts that share the scenario, user prompt, steering condition, and prefill fraction differ pre-action. We trained 10 residual-only configurations per condition (4 single-layer ×\times 2 probe kinds plus 1 multi-layer concat ×\times 2 probe kinds; n≈297n\approx 297 per condition) on the bridging-probe prefill features. Per-condition best AUCs are 0.5930.593 (baseline), 0.5580.558 (calm, α=0.05\alpha=0.05), 0.5750.575 (desperate, α=0.10\alpha=0.10), and 0.6400.640 (random, α=0.10\alpha=0.10); pooled mean 0.5910.591. All three pre-specified gates (per-condition AUC <0.65<0.65, pooled mean <0.65<0.65, no condition AUC >0.75>0.75) pass. Caveat: the random-direction condition’s best AUC of 0.6400.640 is only 0.0100.010 below the gate threshold. This is a condition-controlled prediction check, not an identical-prefix minimal-pair test: the prefill states include rollout-specific truncated assistant prefixes, so the per-row hidden state is not byte-identical across rollouts within a condition.

Four semantic-control directions.

We evaluate four content-coded directions, cats, weather, sports, and geography, extracted by the same difference-of-means plus neutral-PCA pipeline and applied at L41 of Gemma-3-27B-IT under the throughout-steering plugin at the same global steering norm. Sample size is n=300n=300 per condition, and the canonical multi-dimensional alignment judge is reused. Storygen corpus sizes are 493 sports stories, 485 geography stories, 491 weather stories, and 200 cats stories. The smaller cats corpus is an inherited asymmetry from the cats-control run, so diff-of-means estimation is approximately equal-power for sports / geography / weather and noisier for cats.

Pre-specified gates.

The Fisher gates use the pre-specified Bonferroni threshold α′=0.0125\alpha^{\prime}=0.0125; the 4-way omnibus is a separately pre-specified uncorrected α=0.10\alpha=0.10 test. (i) sports0.10 vs random0.10: rejects at p=1.9×10−4p=1.9\times 10^{-4} (OR 0.3570.357, 95% CI [0.207,0.616][0.207,0.616]; RD −10.0-10.0 pp); sports sits significantly below random. (ii) geography0.05 vs calm0.05: rejects at p=4.7×10−3p=4.7\times 10^{-3} (OR 3.073.07, 95% CI [1.41,6.66][1.41,6.66]; RD +5.7+5.7 pp). (iii) 4-way omnibus over weather0.10 / cats0.10 / sports0.10 / geography0.10: rejects equality at p=1.7×10−4p=1.7\times 10^{-4} (χ2=20.03\chi^{2}=20.03, df=3\mathrm{df}=3). (iv) sports0.05 vs cats0.05: does not reject (p=0.175p=0.175); no equivalence margin was pre-specified, so this is a non-rejection rather than an equivalence claim. A protocol-consistency gate on the baseline rate (observed 5.3%5.3\%, target 5.3%±55.3\%\pm 5 pp) passes.

Caveats for the semantic-control sweep.

(a) Geography is near random is descriptive only (17.0%17.0\% vs 16.7%16.7\% at n=300n=300 each, 0.30.3 pp by point estimate); no equivalence test was pre-specified. (b) The heterogeneity claim is scoped to these four tested directions, not the content class generally. (c) This sweep uses T=0.7T=0.7; cross-comparisons against the matched-marginals run, which used T=1.0T=1.0, should be read with that documented protocol divergence in mind. (d) No second-model check was run for sports or geography; cross-model claims for the four-direction semantic-control sweep are out of scope.
